newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Feuding Cambodian leaders agree to end row.
newsitem.headline: Feuding Cambodian leaders agree to end row.

text.p: Cambodia's feuding co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen met for the first time in more than two months on Wednesday and agreed to end their bitter public war of words, a senior government official said.

Ranariddh and Hun Sen, whose rivalry stems partly from their efforts to garner support ahead of national elections next year, co-chaired their first cabinet meeting since March 5, the last time they met.

Verbal sparring between the two over various issues since then has paralysed the coalition government and parliament, analysts said, adding they feared it might be too late to forge a lasting rapprochement between the leaders and their parties.
Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party and the Cambodian People's Party (CPP) of Hun Sen formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
The two were seen smiling and chatting together at the end of the three-hour cabinet meeting on Wednesday.

Cabinet spokesman Sok An told reporters that Ranariddh and Hun Sen had agreed "the government should function normally and from 6:00 p.m. there will be no polemics between the two prime ministers broadcasting through the TV or radio."
However, before the cabinet convened, Ranariddh said:
"The political atmosphere is not very good -- it is quite bad." He was speaking at a ceremony and diplomats said his comments reflected the country's deep political divisions.
Analysts welcomed the decision at the cabinet meeting, but doubted it would be adhered to as the rivals get closer to elections due before the end of next year.
Sok An said the premiers agreed to give full power to Information Minister Ieng Mouly to supervise and control all radio and television stations to ensure an end to their row.

He said it would be impossible to include the partisan print media in the order but indicated that independent radio and television stations loyal to FUNCINPEC or the CPP would be subject to supervision.
"We hope and we wish that it will be fairly implemented," said Sok An.
"It is a very important decision to make sure that political stability is assured. There will be normal functioning of the government," he added.
Ties between the two leaders and their parties began to deteriorate after Ranariddh threated to leave the government in March 1996 in a row over power-sharing.

The ill-feeling simmered for a year, with sniping between the two played out in the country's lively and unruly press, although the two leaders promised to work closely together after the March 5 cabinet meeting.
That truce lasted less than a week and ties have deteriorated further since a deadly March 30 grenade attack on an opposition rally led by FUNCINPEC ally Sam Rainsy.
Relations hit new depths when royalist dissidents challenged Ranariddh's leadership of FUNCINPEC in mid-April and received promises of support from Hun Sen.
The news triggered rumours of an imminent coup that were only allayed when top defence and security officials pledged neutrality at a mass meeting late last month.

On Sunday, gunmen killed one announcer in an attack on a state-run radio studio in the southern city of Sihanoukville. Local police said the incident came after the station chief refused to air a speech by a top royalist.
